questions.qtext:
Let L (x, y) be the statement “x loves y” where the domain for both x and y consists of all people
in the world. Use quantifiers to express “Chaitra is loved by everyone”.
questions.subject: Technical

options.text: Depth-First Search is optimal and uses exponential space.
Depth-Limited Search always finds the least-cost solution.
Uniform Cost Search guarantees the optimal path but may require exponential space.
Random Search is complete and optimal.

questions.solution:
(c)
• Uniform Cost Search (UCS) expands the node with the lowest path cost and guarantees the optimal solution, assuming all step costs are non-negative.
• However, UCS maintains all generated nodes in memory, which can lead to exponential space complexity in the worst case, particularly when the solution cost is high and each action has a small minimum cost ε.
questions.subject: Technical

options.text: Path cost in Uniform Cost Search is used only at the goal node to verify the solution.
Uniform Cost Search prioritizes nodes with higher path cost to ensure completeness.
Path cost refers to the cumulative cost from the start node to the current node and is used to guide the search.
Path cost is irrelevant when all edge costs are the same.

questions.solution:
(c)
• Path cost is not used only at the goal node. In Uniform Cost Search (UCS), the path cost is continuously calculated for every node during the search to decide which node to expand next. So, option (a) is incorrect.
• UCS does not prioritize nodes with higher path cost. Instead, it always expands the node with the lowest cumulative path cost first to ensure the least costly path is found. So, option (b) is incorrect.
• It is the sum of costs along the path from the start node to the current node, and UCS uses this
cumulative cost to prioritize node expansion. So, option (c) is correct.
• Even if all edge costs are equal, UCS still considers path cost to maintain proper ordering.
Thus, path cost is never irrelevant. So, option (d) is incorrect.

questions.qtext: In Greedy Best-First Search, the node to be expanded next is selected based on:

options.text: The lowest cumulative path cost from the start node.
The lowest heuristic estimate of distance to the goal.
The highest path cost from the start node.

questions.solution:
(b)
Greedy Best-First Search is an informed search strategy that expands the node that appears to be closest to the goal, using a heuristic function.
• It uses a heuristic estimate h(n), which estimates the cost from node n to the goal.
• The algorithm selects the node with the lowest heuristic value h(n), assuming that lower h(n)
means closer to the goal.

questions.qtext: In a DFS traversal of a graph, which of the following conditions may lead to incompleteness?

options.text: Finite state space with loop checking
Infinite state space with no loop checking
Use of heuristic in node expansion

questions.solution:
(b)
• DFS is incomplete in infinite state spaces if there’s no loop detection (can go infinitely deep on one path).
• Loop checking is necessary to make DFS complete in finite graphs.

questions.qtext: The first order logic (FOL) statement ((R ∨ Q) ∧ (P ∨ ¬Q)) is equivalent to which of the following?
questions.subject: Technical

options.text: DFS always finds the shortest path faster than BFS in graphs with cycles.
DFS is guaranteed to find a solution in the shortest time possible.
AO* uses breadth-first search on AND-OR graphs ignoring heuristics.
BFS cannot handle infinite-depth search problems.

questions.solution:
(a, b, c)
• DFS does not guarantee finding the shortest path, especially in graphs with cycles. BFS is
preferred for shortest path in unweighted graphs because it explores level-by-level. So,
option (a) is incorrect.
• DFS is not guaranteed to find a solution in the shortest time. It can get stuck going deep into
a branch without finding the goal quickly. So, option (b) is incorrect.
• AO* algorithm works on AND-OR graphs using heuristics to prune and guide the search, not
blindly like breadth-first search. So, option (c) is incorrect.
• BFS explores all nodes level-wise and stores all nodes at each level. In infinite-depth or infinitebranching
problems, BFS can run out of memory or fail to terminate. So, option (d) is correct.
questions.subject: Technical

options.text: Alpha-beta pruning always changes the final decision in a game tree search.
Alpha-beta pruning increases the number of branches traversed in a game tree.
Alpha-beta pruning reduces the number of branches traversed without affecting the solution.
Alpha-beta pruning is used only for single-player games.

questions.solution:
(c)
Alpha-beta pruning is an optimization of the Minmax algorithm used in two-player games. It
reduces the number of branches evaluated by pruning those that cannot affect the final decision,
improving efficiency without changing the result.
Options (a), (b), and (d) are incorrect because alpha-beta pruning does not change the final decision,
does not increase branches searched, and is not used in single-player games.
questions.subject: Technical

options.text: Simple Hill Climbing evaluates all neighbors and selects the best one.
Simple Hill Climbing randomly selects a neighbor to move to.
Simple Hill Climbing evaluates neighbors one by one and selects the first better one.
Simple Hill Climbing stores all neighbors before making a decision.

questions.solution:
(c)
Simple Hill Climbing checks neighbors one by one and moves to the first neighbor that improves
the current state. It does not evaluate all neighbors, does not store them, and does not choose
randomly.
